Going straight to the flaw feels right because praise seems like a delay, and the problem is the part that needs fixing. But watch what happens. Your friend has spent hours on that letter, so a bare list of faults lands like a slap. They stop hearing the typos and start thinking that all you saw in their weekend was the mistakes. Soon a quick fix feels like a stiff little argument.

A barber knows better. He spreads lather over your face before the razor touches it, and the shave feels softer than it would on bare skin. The president Calvin Coolidge did this with words. He praised his secretary's dress first, and only then told her to take more care with her punctuation. The advice behind both is plain: begin with praise and honest appreciation, then raise the problem. The reason is simple, too. People find the unpleasant part easier to hear after they have heard something good. In both cases the good part comes first, so the hard part has somewhere soft to land. That is why the appreciation has to be honest: only praise what you truly value, because a made-up compliment is a cover, and people can tell.

This is why the idea works on a letter, a recipe, or a song. The praise is not a trick to get past anyone. It tells the person you looked at their work and saw something in it, so they can believe you when you say what is wrong. Pick something specific, like the paragraph about their last job, and not just a vague nice job.

So picture your friend watching your face once more. Before you mention one typo, tell them what works in the letter. Then name the typos in a calm voice, and they can hear them. Before you point out a flaw in someone's work, say one true thing you value in it first.
breakdown.fullRead:
Three typos jump off the page of the cover letter your friend wrote all weekend. They stand beside you, waiting to hear what you think. Saying so at once feels honest and quick, and even kind, because why let them send it off with a mistake? You are sure the helpful move is to say it plainly, and you want it over with.

Going straight to the flaw feels right because praise seems like a delay, and the problem is the part that needs fixing. Praise can even feel fake when you are in a hurry, as if you are padding the message to sound nice. Most of us also learned that being direct is being honest, and being honest is being kind. So the quick, plain note feels like the respectful one.

But watch what happens. Your friend has spent hours on that letter, so a bare list of faults lands like a slap. They stop hearing the typos and start thinking that all you saw in their weekend was the mistakes. Soon they are explaining why it was not their fault, and a quick fix turns into a stiff little argument. The typos may get fixed, but the next time they show you their writing, they will show it with their guard up.

Think about a barber. He does not pick up the razor first. He spreads lather over your face, and only then does the blade touch your skin. The shave feels softer than it would on bare skin. Nobody thinks the lather is a waste of the barber's time, because it is part of doing the job well. The lather does not change what the razor does. It changes how the shave feels to you while it happens.

The president Calvin Coolidge used the same idea with words. He praised his secretary's dress first. Only after that did he tell her to take more care with her punctuation. Her dress had nothing to do with commas, but that was not the point. The kind word came first, so the correction came after something good, and not out of nowhere. The advice behind both is plain: begin with praise and honest appreciation, then raise the problem.

The reason is simple: people find the unpleasant part easier to hear after they have heard something good. Remember a time when someone gave you notes on work you cared about. If the first thing you heard was the problem, you probably felt your shoulders tighten, and the rest was hard to take in. When someone is braced for a hit, every word sounds like an attack. A true kind word loosens that brace. Then the correction sounds like help from someone who saw the whole piece of work, and not only its worst spot.

Now for the words themselves. First say the good thing, and make it specific. You might tell your friend that the paragraph about their last job is the clearest part of the letter. Then say the problem as a plain fact: three typos on the first page need to go before it is sent. Keep it short, and stop there. One true thing is enough, and a pile of praise starts to sound like a setup. The same works at home. If your teen's pancakes are burnt on one side, say the batter tastes great, and then ask them to turn the heat down. Remember that the advice asks for honest appreciation, so only praise what you truly value, because a made-up compliment is a cover for the complaint, and people can tell. If nothing comes to mind, look at the work a little longer.

There is a side benefit for you, too. When you look for something to praise before you speak, you slow down and look at the whole piece of work. Often you find it is better than your first glance said, and the flaw looks smaller than it did. Someone who made three typos also wrote a clear paragraph, and you can say both. Then your note comes out calmer and fairer, even before your friend hears a word.

So picture your friend watching your face once more. Before you mention one typo, tell them what works in the letter, and mean it. Then name the typos in a calm voice. They can hear the typos as help, and not as a verdict on their weekend. The praise costs you a few seconds, and it can shape how the whole talk goes. Before you point out a flaw in someone's work, say one true thing you value in it first.

examples.title: A stone path with a gap
examples.scenario: Wanjiru manages a small landscaping crew, and her newest hire, Emre, just finished laying a stone path behind a client's house. The stones are even and the curves are smooth, but he left a gap at the end where mud will wash in. The client arrives in ten minutes, and Wanjiru is about to start with the gap.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Emre the curves are smooth and the stones are even, because they are. Then show him the gap and ask him to fill it before the client comes.
examples.whyItMatters: Emre hears that his careful work was seen, so he takes the gap as a quick fix and not as a verdict.

examples.title: A leaning cardboard roof
examples.scenario: Mina and her studio partner Joon built a cardboard model of a bus station for class. Joon did the roof, and the joins are tidy and the edges are sharp. But the whole roof leans to one side, and the review starts in an hour. Mina feels a joke about the lean rising in her throat.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Joon the joins are the tidiest part of the model. Then point out the lean and ask if the two of you can fix the supports together.
examples.whyItMatters: Joon knows Mina saw the good work, so he stays open to the fix and the pair walk into the review as a team.

examples.title: A toast that runs too long
examples.scenario: Yara's younger brother Teodor wrote a toast for their parents' anniversary dinner and reads it to her in the kitchen. It has a funny story about their dad and a warm closing line. But it runs for nearly ten minutes, and people will be hungry. Teodor looks up from the page, waiting. Yara is about to say it is too long.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Teodor the story about their dad made you laugh, and the closing line moved you. Then say it needs to be shorter and ask which parts he would cut.
examples.whyItMatters: He hears what already works, so he trims with care and keeps the best parts, instead of getting hurt and keeping it all.

questions.prompt: A friend shows you the bookshelf they built from scratch. The wood is smooth, but one shelf sits a little crooked. What do you do?
choices: Say you love the smooth wood, then mention the crooked shelf.
Point out the crooked shelf first, since they would want to know.
Say it looks great overall and leave the crooked shelf for later.
questions.explanation: Naming something true you like first makes the crooked shelf easier to hear. Starting with the flaw makes the work feel unseen, and praise alone hides what they need to know.

questions.prompt: A manager reviews a new hire's first report and says right away, You have two wrong totals. The hire goes quiet and stiff. What belief led the manager wrong?
choices: She thought the hire needed a sterner tone, so a firmer line would have worked.
She thought kind words belong at the end, so closing on praise would have fixed it.
She thought praise wastes time, so she never said what she liked in the report.
questions.explanation: She went straight to the flaw because she saw praise as wasted time. A firmer tone adds more sting, and kind words only at the end leave the first moment cold.

questions.prompt: A father tells his daughter her science poster has great drawings, then says the labels need bigger writing. What happens next?
choices: She feels the praise was only a trick, so she ignores the labels note.
She takes the labels note as help, since she knows her drawings were seen.
She loses interest in the poster, because any note at all will hurt her pride.
questions.explanation: The praise was true and specific, so she knows her work was seen and can hear the labels note as help. A true compliment is not a trick, and a note need not crush her.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, I will just tell the new guy his slides are a mess, because praise only wastes time. What is the best reply?
choices: Fair enough, because a short blunt note respects his time more than kind words.
Say it is good effort in general, then list every problem you can find.
Say one part you truly like first, then raise the real problem with him.
questions.explanation: A true, specific compliment first makes the hard part easier to hear. Blunt notes save little time if he gets defensive, and vague praise sounds like filler with nothing real in it.

questions.prompt: A head cook tells a new line cook the sauce is rich and well seasoned, then says it sat on the heat too long. Why does that order help?
choices: It distracts the new cook, so the hard news does not really sink in.
A hard note is easier to hear after something good has been said.
It makes the new cook like the boss, so every later note gets accepted.
questions.explanation: The good word loosens the listener's guard, so the hard part is heard as help. It is not a distraction, and being liked is only a side effect, not the reason.

questions.prompt: Your roommate hands you the budget sheet they made for splitting rent, and one total is off. The layout is clear and easy to follow. What do you do?
choices: Say the layout is easy to follow, then show them the total that is off.
Fix the total yourself and say nothing, so they never feel bad about it.
Say the totals are wrong right away, before looking at the rest of the sheet.
questions.explanation: One true, specific good word first makes the correction easier to hear. Fixing it silently skips the talk, and going straight to the error puts them on the defense.

questions.prompt: A teacher writes on an essay, Great effort! Now fix your whole second paragraph. The student feels no better. What went wrong?
choices: The teacher praised too little, and a long pile of kind words would have worked.
The praise was vague, so it never showed the teacher saw anything real.
The teacher should have skipped praise, since only the fix matters to the student.
questions.explanation: Vague praise like great effort does not prove the teacher read the work. A specific true thing does. A pile of kind words sounds like a setup, and skipping praise brings back the sting.

reviewCards.front: What comes first when you need to correct a person's work, and why does it help?
reviewCards.back: Say one true thing you value in it first. People hear the unpleasant part more easily after they have heard something good.

reviewCards.front: Your sister baked you a birthday cake, and the middle is raw. What do you say first?
reviewCards.back: Tell her something true you like, such as the frosting or the effort she put in. Then say the middle needs more time in the oven.

reviewCards.front: Why does a true compliment before a correction make the correction easier to take?
reviewCards.back: The unpleasant part is easier to hear after something good. The person is less braced, so the correction sounds like help and not an attack.

reviewCards.front: Before you point out a flaw, say one true thing you ______ in the work, so the hard part is ______ to hear.
reviewCards.back: value, and easier. A real good word first loosens the listener's guard, so they can take in what needs fixing.

reviewCards.front: A coach told a player, Your passing was sloppy, with no kind word first, and the player stopped listening. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The coach went straight to the flaw. Start with one true thing you value in the player's game, then name the passing problem.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before you name a flaw in someone's work, say one specific thing you truly like in it.

ifThenPlans.context: When a coworker asks you to look over their email draft
ifThenPlans.plan: then I say one thing in it that works, such as a clear first line, before I mention any change.

ifThenPlans.context: When my kid shows me homework with a mistake on it
ifThenPlans.plan: then I say one thing they did well, such as neat handwriting, and then point to the mistake.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, think of one thing you meant to correct in someone's work, and send them a short message that opens with one true thing you value in it. It takes under two minutes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each day this week, take two minutes to recall one correction you gave and check whether you opened with something true you valued. Jot a line about how it landed.

chapters.title: Show the better way instead of naming the fault
chapters.hook: How do you fix a mistake without ever saying what the mistake was? Your new helper at the car wash leaves streaks on every window, and you want that fixed without one scolding word.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think the fastest fix is to tell someone exactly what they did wrong. Actually, you get further by showing the right way and letting them see it, because a named fault stings and a shown way leaves their dignity whole.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Fix a mistake by showing the right way, not by naming the fault, so people keep their dignity.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one habit of someone near you that bugs you, and do it the right way, slowly and in plain view, at home or work today. Say nothing, because a shown way shames no one.

memorableLines.text: Show the better way where they can see it, and skip the blame.

breakdown.fastRead:
How do you fix a mistake without ever saying what the mistake was? Say you run a car wash, and your new helper leaves streaks on every window. The scolding is ready in your head, and it feels fair, because the streaks are plain to see.

Naming the fault feels like the fast way, because you say what is wrong and they fix it. But a named fault stings, and a person who is stung starts defending instead of learning. Carnegie's advice is to point out mistakes indirectly, by showing the better way instead of naming the fault. John Wanamaker once saw a customer being ignored while the clerks chatted. He did not scold them. He served her himself, then handed her purchase to the clerks to wrap. They watched the right way done in front of them, and no one was shamed. I would bend this a little: if a hint goes unseen or the mistake could hurt someone, say it plainly and kindly.

So back to the car wash. Skip the scolding, take a clean towel, and wipe one window the right way while your helper watches. Then hand over the towel. Your helper sees the better way, and nobody has to hear a list of faults. When you want a mistake fixed, do it right where the person can see it, and leave their pride alone.
breakdown.deepRead:
How do you fix a mistake without ever saying what the mistake was? Say you run a car wash, and your new helper leaves streaks on every window. The scolding is ready in your head, and it feels fair, because the streaks are plain to see.

Naming the fault feels like the fast way, because you say what is wrong and they fix it. But watch what a named fault does. Your helper feels the sting, and the next minutes go to excuses. The cloth was old, the sun was in the way, nobody showed them how. Even if the windows improve, your helper now wonders what else you are quietly counting against them. A fault said out loud tells a person they were wrong, and almost nobody learns well while feeling small.

Carnegie's advice is to call attention to people's mistakes indirectly, by showing the better way and letting them see it. John Wanamaker once saw a customer being ignored while the clerks chatted. He did not scold them. He served her himself, then handed her purchase to the clerks to wrap. They watched the right way done in front of them, and no one was shamed. Charles Schwab did something like it when he found workers smoking under a No Smoking sign. He gave each one a cigar and asked them to smoke it outside. Neither man named the fault out loud. I would bend this a little: if a hint goes unseen or the mistake could hurt someone, say it plainly and kindly.

Here is why this works. When you show the right way, the person can see the difference with their own eyes, so they do not need your verdict. They also get to change without an audience, because nothing was said about them. Wanamaker's clerks were shown what good service looks like without a word of blame.

So back to the car wash. Skip the scolding, take a clean towel, and wipe one window the right way while your helper watches. Then hand over the towel. Your helper sees the better way, and nobody has to hear a list of faults. When you want a mistake fixed, do it right where the person can see it, and leave their pride alone.
breakdown.fullRead:
How do you fix a mistake without ever saying what the mistake was? Say you run a car wash, and your new helper leaves streaks on every window. The scolding is ready in your head, and it feels fair, because the streaks are plain to see. Your helper has been at it all morning, and the cars keep coming. Waiting feels like a waste of time. Naming the fault seems like the quickest cure.

Naming the fault feels like the fast way, because you say what is wrong and they fix it. It also feels honest, and honesty seems like a good thing to give someone. But watch what a named fault does. Your helper feels the sting, and the next minutes go to excuses. The cloth was old, the sun was in the way, nobody showed them how. Even if the windows improve, your helper now wonders what else you are quietly counting against them. You may even be right about every word. That does not matter much, because being right and being heard are not the same thing. A fault said out loud tells a person they were wrong, and almost nobody learns well while feeling small.

Carnegie's advice is to call attention to people's mistakes indirectly, by showing the better way and letting them see it. A good case is John Wanamaker. He once saw a customer being ignored while the clerks chatted. He did not scold them. He served her himself. Then he handed her purchase to the clerks to wrap.

Think about what the clerks got. They watched a customer get good service, right in front of them, and then they were given the next step of the job. No one named their fault, so no one had to defend it. They could see the gap between what they had been doing and what good service looks like. Notice that the customer also got what she came for, and the fix did not wait for a lesson. Wanamaker let them learn by watching instead of telling them they were bad at it.

Carnegie also tells a story about Charles Schwab. He once found workers smoking under a No Smoking sign. He did not scold them. He gave each one a cigar and asked them to smoke it outside. The sign already said what was not allowed, so he put his words into where to smoke instead. Notice what the two stories share. Neither man said, 'You did this wrong.' Each one changed what was in front of people and let them reach their own conclusion.

Here is Carnegie's reason. Open blame hits a person's pride, and a person whose pride is hit pushes back. It also stirs up resentment, while a shown way lets the person keep their dignity. Think of the last time somebody told you flatly what you did wrong. Your first feeling was probably not thanks. When you point to the better way instead, you leave pride alone, so the person can change without first winning a fight with you.

Here is how it looks in real life. Do the job the right way once, in plain view, and slowly enough that someone can follow. Then hand over the cloth and step back. You can also let your helper wipe the next window while you stand nearby, and say nothing if it comes out clean. The glass answers for you. If you say anything, keep it plain, like 'try it like this.' Skip lines that are really jabs, such as 'Is this how it is supposed to look?' That is blame with a question mark on the end.

I would bend this a little: if a hint goes unseen or the mistake could hurt someone, say it plainly and kindly. Showing also has to be honest. If you wipe the window with a loud sigh, so everyone knows who it is aimed at, that is a scolding in costume. Do it calmly, and mean it as a lesson and not a message of shame.

So back to the car wash. Skip the scolding, take a clean towel, and wipe one window the right way while your helper watches. Then hand over the towel. It costs you one minute of your own time. Your helper sees the better way, and nobody has to hear a list of faults. Some days a spot will still be missed, but nobody has been made to feel small. When you want a mistake fixed, do it right where the person can see it, and leave their pride alone.

examples.title: A flat hello on the pizzeria phone
examples.scenario: Amara runs a pizzeria counter, and the evening rush is on. Her patience is thin. Her new hire, Yaw, answers the phone with a flat 'Yeah?' and callers sound confused. Another call starts ringing. Amara has a line ready: 'You sound rude on the phone.' Yaw glances over and waits for whatever she says.
examples.whatToDo: Answer the ringing phone yourself with a warm greeting and the shop's name, then let Yaw take the next one.
examples.whyItMatters: Yaw hears what a good greeting sounds like and can copy it, with no one having called him rude.

examples.title: A mumbled speech before class
examples.scenario: Petra and Bastien practice for tomorrow's speech class in an empty classroom. Bastien reads his speech to the floor in a quiet mumble, and Petra can barely hear him. 'You're mumbling, and nobody will hear you' is right on the tip of her tongue. He finishes, looks up, and waits for her verdict.
examples.whatToDo: Read his opening line aloud yourself, head up and voice clear, then say, 'Try it like that.' Let him copy you.
examples.whyItMatters: Bastien hears the difference instead of hearing his fault, so he can fix his voice without feeling small.

examples.title: A first video call with the grandchildren
examples.scenario: Farah's father is on his first video call with his grandchildren. He holds the phone low, so all they see is his chin and the ceiling. They giggle, and he looks puzzled. He glances at her for help. Farah sits beside him with her own phone, and the words 'You're holding it wrong' are on her lips.
examples.whatToDo: Lift your own phone to eye level where he can see it, and say, 'Try it up here.' Let him copy you.
examples.whyItMatters: He sees the right way at once and keeps his pride, which makes him more willing to try the next call.

questions.prompt: Your nephew helps at your yard sale and keeps stacking heavy books on top of the boxes of glassware. You are standing beside the table. What do you do?
choices: Tell him that books on top of glass are a careless way to stack.
Restack one box with the books below, then hand him the next one.
Wait until the sale ends, then explain how heavy things should go.
questions.explanation: Restacking in front of him shows the right way without naming a fault, so he can copy it with his pride intact. Calling it careless stings, and explaining later misses the moment he can see.

questions.prompt: A coach watched a new player hold the bat with hands far apart and said, 'Your grip is all wrong.' The player stopped trying new things. Which belief led the coach wrong?
choices: The coach thought naming the fault was fastest, so no better grip was shown.
The coach thought a softer voice would fix it, though the words stayed the same.
The coach thought the player needed more drills before anyone could correct the grip.
questions.explanation: Naming the fault felt quickest, but it stings and shows no better way. A softer voice still names the fault, and more drills skip the fix.

questions.prompt: A flatmate leaves the stove knobs greasy after every meal. Instead of complaining, you wipe your own knobs clean after dinner while they watch. What happens next?
choices: They feel scolded by the silence, so they only clean when you are watching.
They ignore it, because people only change when told exactly what went wrong.
They see the better way and may copy it, with nothing to defend.
questions.explanation: Seeing clean knobs gives them a way to follow and no fault to argue with. It may not work at once, but a shown habit is hard to miss, and it is not a scolding.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, 'The new intern keeps talking over people in meetings, so I'll just tell them they interrupt too much.' What is the best reply?
choices: Go ahead, because saying it plainly saves time and leaves them no room to doubt.
Let others finish in the next meeting, then ask the intern for a view.
Tell them they interrupt, but open with praise first so it lands more softly.
questions.explanation: Showing good listening in the meeting lets the intern see the better way without being named. Plain blame stings, and praise first still ends in naming the fault.

questions.prompt: A manager takes over the register, greets a waiting customer warmly, and then lets the trainee ring up the sale. Why does that work better than telling the trainee off?
choices: It lets the manager look kind, so the trainee will want to please the manager.
It is only a gentle warm-up, and the real fix still has to be said out loud.
It lets the trainee see the better way without being named as the problem.
questions.explanation: Seeing the right way up close gives the trainee something to copy, and no fault is spoken. Looking kind is a side effect, and the fix does not need a spoken fault.

questions.prompt: Your daughter is learning to sew, and her seams keep puckering. You sit beside her at the machine. What do you do?
choices: Sew a few stitches at an easy pace, then slide the fabric to her.
Point at the puckered seam and ask her what she thinks went wrong with it.
Tell her puckered seams happen when she rushes, so she should slow down now.
questions.explanation: Sewing a few stitches shows the right pace in action, so she can copy it. Pointing at the seam and telling her to slow down both name the fault.

questions.prompt: A team lead restacks a crooked pile of chairs while sighing loudly and glancing at the person who stacked them. That person goes quiet. What went wrong?
choices: The lead should have said the fault outright, because showing never works with people.
The sigh and glance named the fault, so the showing became a scolding.
The lead should have restacked every chair, because one pile is too small a lesson.
questions.explanation: The better way was shown, but the sigh and glance pointed at the person, so it still felt like blame. Showing only works when it is calm and not aimed.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how should you handle someone who keeps making the same small mistake, and why?
reviewCards.back: Do it the right way where they can see it, instead of naming the fault. A shown way lets them fix it and keep their pride.

reviewCards.front: Your teenager tosses grocery bags into the trunk with the eggs at the bottom. What is one move that fits?
reviewCards.back: Repack one bag the right way, with heavy things below and eggs on top, then hand over the next bag. No lecture, and your teen keeps their pride.

reviewCards.front: Why does someone often get defensive when you tell them exactly what they did wrong?
reviewCards.back: A named fault stings their pride, so they spend effort defending instead of learning. A shown way gives them something to copy and nothing to argue with.

reviewCards.front: When you correct by showing the right way, you leave the person's ______ whole.
reviewCards.back: Dignity, or pride. They can see the better way and change it without feeling small.

reviewCards.front: A coach saw a player stand flat-footed at serve and said, 'Your stance is lazy.' The player stopped listening. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The coach named the fault and stung the player's pride. Better: take a ready stance yourself and say, 'Try it like this,' so the player can copy it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: When you see a mistake, do the task the right way in plain view instead of naming what was wrong.

ifThenPlans.context: When a coworker leaves a shared document with messy headings
ifThenPlans.plan: then I fix the first heading the way I like it and say, 'I set it up like this, want to keep going?'

ifThenPlans.context: When a child or younger relative holds a pen or tool in an awkward way
ifThenPlans.plan: then I hold mine the better way beside them and say, 'Try it like this,' with no word about what was wrong.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, when someone near you does a small task poorly, take over one step the right way, hand it back, and say only 'Your turn.' It takes under two minutes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening, spend two minutes recalling one moment you wanted to name a fault. Write one line on how you could have shown the better way instead.

chapters.title: Mention your own mistake before you name theirs
chapters.hook: The best way to open a correction is to talk about yourself. What happens when you share a slip of your own before you mention theirs, and why does that help them hear you?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a mistake gets fixed fastest if you point at it and keep your own record out of it. Actually, they listen better when you first name a similar mistake of yours, because they hear a fellow learner, not a critic.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you point out someone's mistake, tell them about a similar mistake you made yourself.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tell the next person you correct today about one similar slip of your own, in a sentence or two, before you name theirs. It shows them you are not above the problem.

memorableLines.text: Name your own slip first, and theirs becomes easy to hear.

breakdown.fastRead:
Start a correction with your own mistake, not the other person's. It sounds backward, because they are the one who needs to change. Say a coworker keeps handing in the weekly sheet with the same error, and you have a sentence ready that begins with 'Once again.'

Pointing straight at the error feels honest and quick, while your own old slips feel like a detour. But your coworker hears only their faults from someone who seems to have none, so they feel small and start defending themselves. Carnegie's niece worked as his secretary and made a mistake. Before he said a word about it, he thought of the far worse blunders he had made at her age. He began with those and only then spoke about hers, so she heard someone who had been where she was, not someone grading her. You can follow Carnegie with one caution: your story must be true and close to theirs, because a made-up one is a trick. A mistake with real costs still has to be named clearly.

So before you say 'Once again,' tell your coworker about a sheet of your own that went out wrong, and what you learned from it. Then name their slip. Go first with a slip of your own, and the person across from you can hear theirs without having to defend themselves.
breakdown.deepRead:
Start a correction with your own mistake, not the other person's. It sounds backward, because they are the one who needs to change. Say a coworker keeps handing in the weekly sheet with the same error, and you have a sentence ready that begins with 'Once again.'

Pointing straight at the error feels honest and quick, while your own old slips feel like a detour. It also feels safer to keep your record out of it, because you want them to see you as the one who knows better. But watch what happens. Your coworker hears only their faults from someone who seems to have none, so they feel small and start defending themselves. They explain, they shrug, or they go quiet and nod, and the same error shows up again next week.

Carnegie went the other way. His niece worked as his secretary and made a mistake. Before he said a word about it, he thought of the mistakes he had made himself, and at her age they had been far worse than hers. He began with those blunders and only then spoke about hers. Notice what that did. She did not hear someone who had never failed. She heard someone who had been where she was, so she could listen as a fellow learner, not as someone being graded. Keep one limit on his move: your story must be true and close to theirs, because a made-up one is a trick. A mistake with real costs still has to be named clearly.

Here is why it works. Most of us hear a correction as a statement about who we are, and the first thing we do is protect ourselves. When you go first, you show that decent people make mistakes, so the mistake stops being a charge and becomes a thing to fix. It is like being the first one into a cold lake. Once you are in and fine, the other person sees that it is safe to follow.

So back to your coworker and the weekly sheet. Before you say 'Once again,' tell them about a sheet of your own that went out wrong, and what you did to catch it next time. Then name their slip, and say what to change. It takes half a minute, and it tells them you are a fellow worker with the same trouble, not someone standing above it. Go first with a slip of your own, and the person across from you can hear theirs without having to defend themselves.
breakdown.fullRead:
Start a correction with your own mistake, not the other person's. It sounds backward, because they are the one who needs to change. Say a coworker keeps handing in the weekly sheet with the same error, and you have a sentence ready that begins with 'Once again.' It feels fair, because the slip is theirs and the fix is theirs too. Why would you bring yourself into it?

Pointing straight at the error feels honest and quick, while your own old slips feel like a detour. It also feels safer to keep your record out of it, because you want them to see you as the one who knows better. A story about your own failure seems to weaken you, and it seems to waste the time you need for the real problem. Most of us hold this belief without ever saying it out loud.

But watch what comes back. Your coworker hears only their faults from someone who seems to have none, so they feel small and start defending themselves. They explain, they shrug, or they go quiet and nod, and the same error shows up again next week. Notice that you set yourself above the problem and them inside it, so all they can do is guard themselves. A person who is busy guarding has little room left to learn.

Carnegie's way was the opposite. His niece worked as his secretary, and she made a mistake. He could have told her what she did wrong and left it there. But before he said a word about it, he thought of the mistakes he had made himself. At her age, his blunders had been far worse than hers.

So he began with his own blunders and only then spoke about hers. That order is the whole point. She did not hear someone who had never failed. She heard someone who had been where she was, so she could listen as a fellow learner, not as someone being graded. That kind of opening quietly tells a person that a mistake like theirs does not mark them as hopeless. The honest version of his move asks one thing more: your story must be true and close to theirs, because a made-up one is a trick. A mistake with real costs still has to be named clearly.

Here is why it works. Most of us hear a correction as a statement about who we are, and the first thing we do is protect ourselves. When you go first, you show that decent people make mistakes, so the mistake stops being a charge and becomes a thing to fix. It is like being the first one into a cold lake. Once you are in and fine, the other person sees that it is safe to follow. Without you in the water, they stand on the shore and look for a reason not to jump.

In practice it takes three short moves. Pick one slip of yours that is close to theirs, and say it in a sentence or two. It might sound like this: 'I once sent a sheet out with the wrong totals, and I had to call everyone to fix it.' Then turn to them, and name the slip you noticed in a calm voice. Add what you do now to catch it, because a fix gives them something to try. Keep your story short, since the talk is about their work, not your memories.

A few cautions keep this honest. Do not pick a mistake that is tiny next to theirs, because it will sound like you are brushing the problem off. Do not use the same story on everyone, since people can tell when a confession has been rehearsed. And do not stretch your story into a long speech, because then you have only moved the spotlight onto yourself. The goal is a true moment that tells the other person you are on the same side while you ask for a change.

So back to your coworker and the weekly sheet. Before you say 'Once again,' tell them about a sheet of your own that went out wrong, and what you did to catch it next time. Then name their slip, and say what to change. It takes half a minute, and it tells them you are a fellow worker with the same trouble, not someone standing above it. Some days they will still bristle a little. Even then, you have given them a reason to hear you out, because you went first. Go first with a slip of your own, and the person across from you can hear theirs without having to defend themselves.

examples.title: A split bag of dog food
examples.scenario: Yewande manages a pet supply stockroom. A new hire named Lazar stacked heavy dog food bags on a high shelf, and one bag has split open on the floor. Yewande remembers dropping a whole box of glass jars during her own first month. A sharp line is ready: "Why would you stack those up there?" Lazar looks down at the mess.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Lazar about the glass jars you dropped, then show him which shelves hold heavy bags. Clean up together.
examples.whyItMatters: Lazar hears someone who has been there, so he can take in the shelf rule without feeling small.

examples.title: A cart of books on the wrong shelves
examples.scenario: Camila leads the student volunteers at the school library desk. Ayaan, a new volunteer, shelved a whole cart of returned books in the wrong section. Last term, Camila did the very same thing and had to stay late to fix it. Now she is about to say, "Did you even look at the labels?" while Ayaan waits.
examples.whatToDo: Say you shelved a whole cart wrong last term and stayed late fixing it. Then show Ayaan how the section labels work.
examples.whyItMatters: Ayaan learns the mistake is common and fixable, so he will ask when unsure, not hide the next one.

examples.title: A scraped bumper in an empty lot
examples.scenario: Matthias is teaching his daughter Sanna to drive in an empty lot. She rolls too close and scrapes the bumper on a cart return. Matthias remembers scraping his own father's car on a gatepost at about her age. His first words are ready: "Watch where you're going!" Sanna grips the wheel.
examples.whatToDo: Tell her about the gatepost first, in a few words, then say how to judge the gap next time.
examples.whyItMatters: She hears that her dad once did this too, so she stays calm enough to take in the tip.

questions.prompt: You run a tool library, and a new volunteer lent out a drill without writing it in the log, so no one knows where it is. You are about to talk to the volunteer. What do you do?
choices: Say plainly that the drill is missing and the log must be filled in every time.
Describe a time you skipped the log yourself, then show how you fill it in.
Say that everyone is new once, then let the missing drill go for now.
questions.explanation: Your own skipped log shows you have been there, so the volunteer can listen as a fellow learner. Saying it flatly invites a defense, and comfort alone never fixes the habit.

questions.prompt: A ferry captain told a new deckhand, 'You tied that rope badly, and I never tie one like that.' The deckhand went quiet and stopped asking questions. What was the trap?
choices: The captain was too soft, and a sterner line would have fixed it.
The captain spoke up too soon, before the deckhand had a chance to explain.
The captain claimed to be perfect, so the deckhand could only feel small.
questions.explanation: Claiming you never err leaves the deckhand feeling small and shut out. A harsher line only adds to the defense, and speaking up soon is fine if you own a similar slip first.

questions.prompt: A film club organizer tells a member, 'I once forgot to book the room for a whole screening. Now, about the tickets you forgot to print.' What happens next?
choices: The member relaxes and starts talking about how to print the tickets in time.
The member sees the story as a stall and gets annoyed about the wasted time.
The member decides the missing tickets were not a problem, so nothing changes.
questions.explanation: Hearing a true, similar slip first makes the member feel like a fellow learner, so they drop their guard and start fixing. The story does not erase the problem, and it is not a stall.

questions.prompt: A friend says, 'My brother keeps leaving the garage door open overnight. I'll just tell him it's dangerous and he needs to stop.' What is the best reply?
choices: Go ahead and say it straight, because a direct warning gets the quickest result.
Hint at it with a joke, because a direct warning might hurt his feelings.
Mention the night you left your own door open, then ask him to close it.
questions.explanation: Your own open door shows he is not alone in this slip, so he can hear the danger without feeling attacked. A joke hides the point, and a flat warning invites a defense.

questions.prompt: A tutor tells a student about a time the tutor wrote a wrong answer on the board, then points out the student's slip. Why does this work better than pointing at it directly?
choices: It makes no real difference, because pointing straight at the slip works just as well.
It shows the tutor has slipped too, so the student can listen without defending.
It softens the student up first, so the tutor can then be blunt without pushback.
questions.explanation: Hearing that the tutor slipped too makes the student a fellow learner, not a target. It is not a softening trick, and pointing straight at the slip invites a defense.

questions.prompt: A member of your knitting circle keeps returning the shared pattern books late, and you will raise it on the phone tonight. What do you do?
choices: Start with a time you returned one late, then ask them to bring the books on time.
Start by listing each meeting where the books came back late, then ask for a change.
Start by saying you hate to nag and may be too picky, then ask about the books.
questions.explanation: Your own late book shows you have done the same thing, so they can listen without defending. A list of their misses invites a defense, and apologizing for asking tells them nothing real.

questions.prompt: A project lead tells an intern, 'I made this same mistake once,' but the intern later learns the lead never did. What was the trap?
choices: Mentioning any past mistake makes a lead look weak, so the intern lost respect.
The story was made up as a tool, so it felt like a trick, not honesty.
The lead told the story too late, so the intern had already stopped listening.
questions.explanation: A confession only helps if it is true. An invented one is a trick, and people sense it. Owning a real mistake does not weaken a lead, and timing was not the issue.

reviewCards.front: Before you point out someone's mistake, what is your first move, and why does it help?
reviewCards.back: Tell them about a similar mistake of yours first. They hear a fellow learner, not a critic, so they can listen instead of defend.

reviewCards.front: Your teen left the oven on again after baking, and you need to talk about it. What is your first move?
reviewCards.back: Tell them about a time you left something on, then bring up the oven. Hearing it from someone who has done it too keeps them listening.

reviewCards.front: Why does a correction sound harsher when the person giving it seems to have never made a mistake?
reviewCards.back: The listener hears only their own faults and feels small. Feeling small makes them defend themselves, so the fix gets lost.

reviewCards.front: Going first with your own slip lets the other person listen instead of ______ themselves.
reviewCards.back: defending. When you admit a similar slip, they no longer feel singled out, so they can focus on the fix.

reviewCards.front: A coach told a player, 'I never miss a pass like that.' The player stopped listening. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The coach claimed to be flawless and kept their own record out of it. A true, similar miss shared first would have made the player feel less alone.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before you name someone's mistake, tell them in a sentence or two about a similar mistake of your own.

ifThenPlans.context: When I am about to send a message that starts with 'You forgot' or 'You missed'
ifThenPlans.plan: then I delete that start and write one sentence about a similar slip of mine before I name theirs.

ifThenPlans.context: When a family member leaves a chore half done and sharp words come to mind
ifThenPlans.plan: then I say 'I did the same thing last week,' give the true example, and then ask for the fix.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before bed tonight, pick one slip you made this month and say it aloud in one sentence. Then a true story is ready the next time you need to correct someone.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Sunday evening, name two small mistakes you made that week and one thing each taught you. Keep them ready as true stories to share before a correction.

chapters.title: Turn your orders into questions
chapters.hook: Guests arrive at six and the spare room is half painted, so you bark at your brother to roll the other way. He sighs and slows down. What would have kept him moving?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think that when you are in charge, telling people exactly what to do is the quickest, clearest way to get it done. Actually, a question gets more done, because people feel less pushed around when you ask for their view.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Turn your next order into a question, because people feel less pushed around when you ask for their view.
chapters.tryThisNow: Change one order into a question the next time you hand someone a task today, such as 'Could we start with the front shelf?' It takes five seconds, and it leaves them room to own the job.

memorableLines.text: Put your order as a question and people take the job on as theirs.

breakdown.fastRead:
Guests arrive at six, and the spare room is only half painted. Your brother is rolling the wall the slow way, so you call out, 'Roll it the other way!' It feels clear and quick, and you are the one who knows the clock.

Orders feel right because they seem fast, and being in charge seems to mean you decide. But an order tells a person that their own head is not needed, so they do the task and keep their ideas to themselves. Carnegie passes on the word of a man who worked near Owen D. Young for years and never once heard him give a direct order. Young used suggestions and questions, such as asking what someone thought of a plan or whether it could be done another way. The reason is that a question leaves a person's pride whole, and people carry out more gladly what they helped decide. You need not stretch this too far: in an emergency a plain order is right, and a question with a fixed answer fools nobody.

So back in the spare room, try asking, 'Would it go faster if you rolled it the other way?' Your brother can say yes, or tell you the roller is stuck, and either way he is working with you. When you want something done, put it as a question, and the job starts to feel like theirs.
breakdown.deepRead:
Guests arrive at six, and the spare room is only half painted. Your brother is rolling the wall the slow way, so you call out, 'Roll it the other way!' It feels clear and quick, and you are the one who knows the clock.

Orders feel right because they seem fast, and being in charge seems to mean you decide. When you know the deadline, saying exactly what to do saves you the trouble of explaining. But watch what your brother hears. An order tells him that his own head is not needed, so he does the task and keeps his ideas to himself. Nobody likes to feel pushed around, even for a good reason.

Carnegie passes on the word of a man who worked near Owen D. Young for years and never once heard him give a direct order. Young used suggestions and questions instead, such as asking what someone thought of a plan or whether it could be done another way. Carnegie's point is that this leaves a person's pride whole. It also invites their ideas, and people carry out more gladly what they helped decide. You do not have to match Young's never, though: in an emergency a plain order is right, and a question with a fixed answer fools nobody.

Think about why this works. When you ask, 'What do you think of this?' the other person has to think about the job, not just hear it. They look for the best way, and they may spot a trouble you missed. Then the plan is partly theirs, and people do not push back on their own plan. The order, by contrast, gives them nothing to hold but your wish.

So back in the spare room, try asking, 'Would it go faster if you rolled it the other way?' Your brother can say yes, or tell you the roller is stuck, and either way he is working with you. The question costs a few seconds, and it tells him you want his head, not just his arm. When you want something done, put it as a question, and the job starts to feel like theirs.
breakdown.fullRead:
Guests arrive at six, and the spare room is only half painted. Your brother is rolling the wall the slow way, with short careful strokes, and the clock on your phone keeps moving. You call out, 'Roll it the other way!' It feels clear and quick, and you are the one who knows the deadline. Nothing in you says to stop. You are sure a short, plain order is the fastest help you can give.

Orders feel right because they seem fast, and being in charge seems to mean you decide. When you know the deadline, saying exactly what to do saves you the trouble of explaining. But watch what your brother hears. An order tells him that his own head is not needed, so he does the task and keeps his ideas to himself. Nobody likes to feel pushed around, even for a good reason. An order works on a machine, because you press a button and it moves. People are not buttons. He may do what you said, but his mind goes quiet, and the next idea he has stays in his pocket.

Carnegie tells of Owen D. Young, a famous businessman. A man who worked near him for years said he never once heard Young give anyone a direct order. Young used suggestions and questions instead. A plan came with a question, such as what the other person thought of it, or whether it could be done another way. That is the whole habit, and it fits in one short sentence.

Carnegie's reason is simple. A question leaves a person's pride whole, because they are being asked, not commanded. It also invites their ideas, and people carry out more gladly what they helped decide. A leader who asks still knows what needs doing. The only change is who gets to feel the job is theirs.

Think about it from the other side. Picture a boss who tells you to move a stack of files to the left shelf. You do it. Now picture a boss who asks, 'Where do you think these would be easiest to find?' You stop and think, and you may put them somewhere better than the boss would have. You will also remember where you put them, because you chose the spot. The first job was done to you, and the second was done by you. The same holds at home. 'Take out the trash' gets a sigh, but 'Would you take out the trash before dinner, or is after better?' gets a choice, and a choice feels like respect.

Here is what that looks like on an ordinary day. Instead of 'Move the meeting to ten,' you say, 'Would ten work better for you?' Instead of 'Do it my way,' you say, 'What do you think of doing it this way?' Instead of 'Fix the sign,' you say, 'How would you fix the sign?' Then stop talking and listen. If the answer is better than your plan, use it. If it is not, you can still add what you know, and now you are building together.

No one needs to take this as far as Young did: in an emergency a plain order is right, and a question with a fixed answer fools nobody. If a pan is on fire, nobody needs to be asked what they think. And if you have already decided, do not say 'Don't you think you should...?' People hear the order inside it, and they feel tricked as well as pushed. Ask only when you are ready for a different answer, because a question you will not listen to is just an order in a nicer voice.

So back in the spare room, try asking, 'Would it go faster if you rolled it the other way?' Your brother can say yes, or tell you the roller is stuck, and either way he is working with you. The question costs a few seconds, and it tells him you want his head, not just his arm. He might even have a quicker idea than yours.

That is a small change in words, and it changes what your brother feels. He is no longer being moved around the room. He is helping finish a job with you, and a person who is helping cares more than a person who is obeying. When you want something done, put it as a question, and the job starts to feel like theirs.

examples.title: Sweeping while clients wait
examples.scenario: Tessa owns a hair salon, and Saturday is booked solid. She sees the new stylist, Rhys, sweeping hair from the floor while three clients wait at the shampoo bowls. She has an order ready: 'Stop sweeping and start shampooing.' He looks up, waiting for her to speak.
examples.whatToDo: Ask, 'With three clients waiting, what do you think we should do first?' Listen, then agree on the next few jobs together.
examples.whyItMatters: He may know which client is ready, and a plan he helped shape is one he will carry out gladly.

examples.title: A dark sky on the gym wall
examples.scenario: Fatima leads a class team painting a mural on the gym wall. With one day left, she sees Olumide painting the sky dark gray, and she thinks it will clash with the rest. She is about to say, 'Paint that over with light blue.' He steps back from the wall, brush in hand, looking pleased.
examples.whatToDo: Ask, 'How do you think this gray will look next to the rest?' Listen well, then decide together what the sky needs.
examples.whyItMatters: He may spot the clash on his own, and a fix he picks is one he will finish with his pride whole.

examples.title: A trunk that will not close
examples.scenario: Marisol is packing the trunk for a beach day with her teenage son, Anton. He is stacking the cooler on top of the umbrella, and she can see the lid will not close. The order is on her tongue: 'Take it out and do it my way.' He looks up, already tired of being told.
examples.whatToDo: Ask, 'What do you think will fit better in here?' Let him try his idea, and add yours only if the lid still will not close.
examples.whyItMatters: He gets to solve it, so he stays with you instead of sulking, and the trunk closes without a sour mood.

questions.prompt: You lead volunteers at an animal shelter, and the dog run needs hosing before visitors come. A new volunteer is standing around. What do you do?
choices: Tell the volunteer, 'Hose down the dog run first, then fill the water bowls, and be quick.'
Ask the volunteer, 'The dog run needs hosing before visitors come, where would you start?'
Mutter that the dog run is a mess and sigh, hoping the volunteer takes the hint.
questions.explanation: A real question gives the volunteer a say and keeps their pride whole, so they take the job on. A barked order feels pushy, and a sigh is a hint with no question in it.

questions.prompt: A manager asks a designer, 'Could you make the logo bigger?' When the designer offers another idea, the manager snaps, 'No, bigger.' The designer goes quiet. What belief led the manager wrong?
choices: The manager thought asking makes a leader look weak, so a firmer, louder order would have worked.
The manager thought the designer was slow, so adding a hard deadline would have worked better.
The manager thought a polite tone was enough, but the question had a fixed answer.
questions.explanation: The question was an order wearing a polite tone, because the answer was already set. The designer felt tricked as well as pushed. Asking only works when you will really listen.

questions.prompt: A captain of a pickup ultimate frisbee team asks, 'We keep dropping the disc on the left side. What could we try on Saturday?' instead of announcing a plan. What happens next?
choices: The players offer ideas, and they work harder at the plan they helped shape.
The players hear weakness and lose respect, so the captain must start giving orders again.
The players only name safe ideas, so the captain has to announce the real plan anyway.
questions.explanation: When people help shape a plan, they carry it out more willingly. Asking does not make a leader weak, and a real question can draw out ideas the leader did not have.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, 'My new hire keeps stacking boxes the wrong way. I'll just tell her exactly how, every single time.' What is the best reply?
choices: Go ahead, because telling her exactly how, every single time, is the clearest and quickest fix.
Restack them after she leaves, because that spares her any bad feeling.
Ask how she thinks they stack best, because she may bring an idea you can use.
questions.explanation: Asking invites her view and keeps her pride whole, so she is likelier to stack them well. Orders every time make her feel pushed, and quietly redoing her work teaches her nothing.

questions.prompt: A leader asks, 'What do you think of this plan?' and the team puts more effort into it than into plans handed down. Why does asking work better?
choices: It tricks people into feeling they chose, so they feel they must agree with the leader.
It leaves their pride whole and lets them shape the plan, so it feels like theirs.
It shows the leader has no firm plan, so everyone has to step up to fill the gap.
questions.explanation: People feel less pushed around when asked, and they carry out more gladly what they helped decide. It is not a trick, and the leader can still hold a plan while asking.

questions.prompt: Your ten-year-old has left muddy cleats on the kitchen floor after practice, and guests are coming in an hour. What do you do?
choices: Ask, 'Where do you think these cleats should go so the floor stays clean?'
Snap, 'Cleats on the shelf, right now,' and count to three out loud so they hurry.
Pick them up yourself, sigh loudly, and say nothing so you do not start a fight.
questions.explanation: A question about where lets your child own the fix and keeps their pride whole. Snapping gets obeying at best, and a silent sigh teaches nothing and builds resentment.

questions.prompt: A supervisor tells each worker exactly how to stack the shelves, and they do it. Nobody mentions the leak above the shelves until the boxes are wet. What belief led the supervisor wrong?
choices: That workers speak up when a notice is posted on the wall, so a notice would have fixed it.
That giving exact orders gets the best work, so nobody was ever asked what they saw.
That a louder voice makes orders clearer, so shouting would have helped them listen.
questions.explanation: Exact orders left no room for the workers' own eyes and ideas, so the leak went unmentioned. Asking what they see invites them to speak, and a notice or a louder voice does not.

reviewCards.front: Before you give your next order, what change should you make to it, and why?
reviewCards.back: Turn it into a question that asks for the person's view. People feel less pushed around, so they carry the job out more gladly.

reviewCards.front: Your teenager's laundry basket has sat at the top of the stairs all day, and you want it moved. What do you say?
reviewCards.back: Ask, 'What do you think is the best time to move this?' A real question gives them a say, and they are likelier to do it.

reviewCards.front: Why does 'What do you think of this plan?' get more effort than 'Do it this way'?
reviewCards.back: The question leaves their pride whole and invites their ideas. People carry out more gladly what they helped decide.

reviewCards.front: A question you have already answered in your head is just an ______ in a nicer ______.
reviewCards.back: Order, in a nicer voice. People hear it, so they feel tricked as well as pushed. Ask only when you are ready to listen.

reviewCards.front: A shop owner told a new clerk, 'Move the display and put the red ones in front.' The clerk did it, but never said the sun faded the red ones there. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The owner gave an order, so the clerk had no room to share what they saw. Asking 'Where do you think these would look best?' invites that.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: When you need something done, say it as a question that asks for the other person's view.

ifThenPlans.context: When I am about to say 'Do this' to a coworker or classmate
ifThenPlans.plan: then I stop and ask, 'What do you think of doing it this way?' and listen to the whole answer.

ifThenPlans.context: When I want a family member to do a chore
ifThenPlans.plan: then I ask, 'What time works best for you to get this done?' instead of telling them to do it now.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one person you often tell what to do, and this evening ask them one question about a task before you say how you want it done. It takes under two minutes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, take two minutes to write down one order you gave and the question you could have asked instead.

chapters.title: Offer a new role when you must move someone
chapters.hook: Say you must tell someone who has run a team for years to step aside. Is there any way to say it so they leave thanking you, not hating you?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think that when someone must be moved or demoted, the news is bad anyway, so the wording hardly matters. Actually, a hurt to their pride lasts longer than the job, so how you do it matters most.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you must move someone out of a job, offer a new role that lets them keep their pride.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one sentence today that starts with what the person keeps or gains, before the part they lose. Plan to say it in private, not in front of others, because a private word protects their pride.

memorableLines.text: Take the job if you must, but leave the person a place to stand.

breakdown.fastRead:
Here is a puzzle. You must take a team away from someone who has led it for years, and you want that person to walk out of the room still on your side. Is that even possible? Most people say no, because the news is bad whatever you do.

That belief feels true because a loss is a loss. If the job is going, the words around it seem like decoration. But the person loses more than a job. They feel their standing drop, and that sting is the part they remember. General Electric once needed to move the engineer Steinmetz out of the job of department head. It did not simply pull the chair out. It gave Steinmetz a new title, consulting engineer, and Steinmetz was pleased. The company got the change it wanted, and no one was hurt in the getting. The advice is blunt: when you must correct, demote or overrule someone, do it in private and leave them their dignity. Hurting a person's pride is a wrong, and they will not forget it. Stop short of dressing it up, though: a fine title that hides the truth is a trick, so make the new role real and say plainly what is changing.

So back to the team you must take from someone. Do not only pull their chair away, but set out another one. When a person has to leave a job, offer a new role that lets them keep their pride.

That belief feels true because a loss is a loss. If the job is going, the words around it seem like decoration, and a flat announcement feels like the honest way. But picture the person on the receiving end. They lose a job, yes, but they also feel their standing fall, and they wonder what everyone else will think. Notice that the job and the standing are two different losses. The first you may have to cause. The second you do not, and it is the one a person remembers longest.
